summary.text: Run-length identities yield recurrences \(\ell_{m+1}=\ell_m+r_m\), \(r_{m+1}=r_m+q_m-1\), and \(q_{m+5}=q_{m+4}+\ell_m\), with \(0\le q_m\le r_m\le \ell_m\); for the root \(1<\lambda<2\) of \(\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1\), a positive weighted combination of these quantities satisfies an affine first-order recurrence, giving \(c\lambda^m\le \ell_m\le C\lambda^m\). The relation \(a_{m+1}=a_m+\ell_m\) then gives analogous two-sided geometric bounds for \(a_m\), and taking \(m\)-th roots and squeezing shows convergence to \(\lambda\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(R\) denote the run-length operator on finite lists: if
\[
X=(x_1,\ldots,x_s),
\]
then \(R(X)\) is the list of lengths of the consecutive maximal blocks of equal entries in \(X\). Put \(R(\varnothing)=\varnothing\).

We use the following indexing of the triangle rows. Define
\[
T_0=\varnothing,\qquad T_1=(1),\qquad T_2=(1),\qquad T_3=(2),
\]
and, for \(n\geq 3\), define
\[
T_{n+1}=R(T_n^{\rm rev})\,T_n,
\tag{1}
\]
where juxtaposition means concatenation and “rev” means reversal. Since reversing a list reverses the order of its runs without changing their lengths,
\[
R(X^{\rm rev})=R(X)^{\rm rev}.
\tag{2}
\]
Thus (1) can equivalently be written
\[
T_{n+1}=R(T_n)^{\rm rev}T_n.
\tag{3}
\]
These are exactly the rows in the recursive description of A381587, and the sequence in question is
\[
a_n=\sum T_n.
\tag{4}
\]
The harmless value at \(n=0\) does not affect a limit as \(n\to\infty\).

We will prove that \(a_n^{1/n}\) tends to a real number \(\lambda>1\).

## 1. Elementary run-length facts

We first record the list identities used below.

For every finite list \(X\),
\[
\sum R(X)=|X|,
\tag{5}
\]
because the runs partition the entries of \(X\). In particular, every entry of \(R(X)\) is positive. If \(\rho(X)=|R(X)|\) is the number of runs of \(X\), then
\[
\rho(X)\leq |X|.
\tag{6}
\]
Indeed, by (5), \(|X|\) is the sum of the \(\rho(X)\) positive run lengths.

If nonempty lists \(A,B\) are concatenated, all runs remain unchanged except possibly the last run of \(A\) and the first run of \(B\). Consequently,
\[
\rho(AB)=
\begin{cases}
\rho(A)+\rho(B)-1,&\text{if the last entry of }A\text{ equals the first entry of }B,\\
\rho(A)+\rho(B),&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
At the level of the entire run-length list, if the boundary entries differ then
\[
R(AB)=R(A)R(B),
\tag{8}
\]
while if they agree, the last entry of \(R(A)\) and first entry of \(R(B)\) are replaced by their sum. These statements follow directly by separating the initial maximal constant block and then continuing inductively through the list. The same description also proves (2).

Equation (5), applied to (3), gives the useful recurrence for row sums:
\[
a_{n+1}=a_n+|T_n|\qquad(n\geq 3).
\tag{9}
\]
Indeed, the newly prefixed list is \(R(T_n)^{\rm rev}\), whose sum is \(|T_n|\).

## 2. Stable boundary data

The main combinatorial point is that, from a finite stage onward, enough of the beginning of \(T_n\) and the end of \(R(T_n)\) stabilize to control all concatenation boundaries.

Introduce the two explicit lists
\[
\begin{aligned}
P={}&(1,3,1,3,1,3,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,1,1,7,1,3,1,1,1,1,1,7),\\
S={}&(7,1,1,1,1,1,3,1,7,1,1,1,1,1,5,1,1,1,3,1,3,1,3,1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Notice that \(S=P^{\rm rev}\).

A direct expansion of the recursion through row \(12\) gives
\[
T_{12}=P D_{12},
\qquad
R(T_{12})=M_{12}S
\tag{11}
\]
for some list \(D_{12}\) and some nonempty list \(M_{12}\). This finite calculation is performed simply by repeatedly reversing a row, taking its consecutive run lengths, and concatenating; its role is only to establish the displayed prefix and suffix. The same expansion gives
\[
|T_{12}|=102.
\tag{12}
\]

The boundary pattern in (11) propagates. More precisely, for every \(n\geq12\), there are lists \(D_n,M_n\), with \(M_n\neq\varnothing\), such that
\[
T_n=P D_n,
\qquad
R(T_n)=M_nS.
\tag{13}
\]
To see this, suppose (13) holds at stage \(n\). By (3),
\[
T_{n+1}=R(T_n)^{\rm rev}T_n=S^{\rm rev}M_n^{\rm rev}T_n
=P M_n^{\rm rev}T_n,
\]
so \(T_{n+1}\) again begins with \(P\).

It remains to check the suffix of \(R(T_{n+1})\). The first entry of \(T_n\) is \(1\), since the first entry of \(P\) is \(1\). Also, because the first two entries of \(P\) are \(1,3\), the first run of \(T_n\) has length \(1\). Thus the last entry of \(R(T_n)^{\rm rev}\) is also \(1\), and at the concatenation boundary in
\(R(T_n)^{\rm rev}T_n\), two runs of the value \(1\) merge. Everything after the first run of \(T_n\) remains unchanged in the run encoding. Since \(R(T_n)=M_nS\) with \(M_n\neq\varnothing\), that unchanged tail still ends in \(S\). The part before it is nonempty, so it supplies a new \(M_{n+1}\). This proves (13) by induction.

We also need a simpler terminal fact. Directly at row \(5\), and hence at every later row because (3) appends the whole preceding row, one has
\[
T_m=W_m(1,2)\qquad(m\geq5)
\tag{14}
\]
for some list \(W_m\). In particular all \(T_m\) with \(m\geq3\) are nonempty.

## 3. The triple run-length identity

We next derive the structural identity that produces the delayed recurrence.

Here is the relevant general run calculation. Suppose a nonempty list \(X\) begins with \(1\), and suppose
\[
R(X)=1^B A,
\tag{15}
\]
where \(1^B\) denotes \(B\) consecutive copies of \(1\), \(B\geq3\), and \(A\neq\varnothing\). Assume also:

1. the first entry of \(A\) is not \(1\);
2. the first entry of \(R(A)\) is none of \(B-1,B,B+1\);
3. the first entry of \(R^2(A)\) is not \(1\).

Then direct use of the boundary rules (8) gives
\[
R^3\bigl(R(X)^{\rm rev}X\bigr)
=R^4(X)^{\rm rev}R^3(X).
\tag{16}
\]
For completeness, we spell out the three run encodings. Since \(X\) begins with \(1\), its first run has length \(1\), which is also the last entry of \(R(X)^{\rm rev}\). Thus the two boundary runs merge. Using (15), one obtains
\[
R\bigl(R(X)^{\rm rev}X\bigr)
=R(A)^{\rm rev}(B+1)1^{B-1}A.
\tag{17}
\]
The first-entry assumptions ensure that no unintended merge occurs at either displayed boundary. Applying \(R\) again gives
\[
R^2\bigl(R(X)^{\rm rev}X\bigr)
=R^2(A)^{\rm rev}(1,B-1)R(A),
\tag{18}
\]
and applying it a third time gives
\[
R^3\bigl(R(X)^{\rm rev}X\bigr)
=R^3(A)^{\rm rev}(1,1)R^2(A).
\tag{19}
\]
On the other hand, encoding (15) itself repeatedly, under the same no-merge assumptions, gives
\[
R^3(X)=(1)R^2(A),

d\qquad
R^4(X)=(1)R^3(A).
\]
Reversing the second identity and concatenating with the first turns the right side into exactly (19), proving (16).

We now verify that this calculation applies to every \(T_n\), \(n\geq12\). From the prefix \(P\) in (13), write
\[
R(T_n)=1^6A_n.
\tag{20}
\]
More explicitly, if \(E_n=R((7)D_n)\), calculation of the runs in the displayed fixed prefix gives
\[
A_n=(3,1,5,1,1,1,5)E_n.
\tag{21}
\]
Therefore \(A_n\) begins with \(3\), and
\[
R(A_n)=(1,1,1,3)R((5)E_n),
\tag{22}
\]
so its first entry is \(1\), which is different from \(5,6,7\). Encoding once more,
\[
R^2(A_n)=(3)R((3)R((5)E_n)),
\tag{23}
\]
so its first entry is \(3\), not \(1\). Thus all hypotheses above hold with \(B=6\). By (3) and (16), for every \(n\geq12\),
\[
R^3(T_{n+1})=R^4(T_n)^{\rm rev}R^3(T_n).
\tag{24}
\]

The next exact identity converts (24) back to earlier rows:
\[
R^3(T_n)=\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{n-4})(6)
\qquad(n\geq12).
\tag{25}
\]
At \(n=12\), this is another direct finite calculation from the recursively generated rows. Only this displayed equality is needed from that calculation.

We prove propagation from \(n=p\) to \(n=p+1\). By (14), write
\[
T_{p-4}=W(1,2).
\]
Then
\[
\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{p-4})(6)=W(1,6).
\]
Because \(6\neq1\) and \(2\neq1\), both \(W(1,6)\) and \(W(1,2)\) have the same run-length encoding: in either case the final entry starts a new singleton run. Hence the induction hypothesis (25) implies
\[
R^4(T_p)=R(T_{p-4}).
\tag{26}
\]
Substitute (26) and the induction hypothesis into (24):
\[
R^3(T_{p+1})
=R(T_{p-4})^{\rm rev}\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{p-4})(6).
\tag{27}
\]
But by (3),
\[
T_{p-3}=R(T_{p-4})^{\rm rev}T_{p-4}.

d\]
Since \(T_{p-4}\neq\varnothing\), deleting the last entry yields
\[
\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{p-3})
=R(T_{p-4})^{\rm rev}\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{p-4}).
\]
This turns (27) into (25) at \(p+1\), completing the induction.

## 4. A delayed linear system for row lengths

Define
\[
\ell_n=|T_n|,
\qquad r_n=|R(T_n)|,
\qquad q_n=|R^2(T_n)|.
\tag{28}
\]
For all \(n\geq12\), these quantities satisfy
\[
\ell_{n+1}=\ell_n+r_n,
\tag{29}
\]
\[
r_{n+1}=r_n+q_n-1,
\tag{30}
\]
and
\[
q_{n+5}=q_{n+4}+\ell_n.
\tag{31}
\]

Equation (29) follows immediately by taking lengths in (3).

For (30), observe from the stable prefix that the first run of \(T_n\) has length \(1\). Thus the last entry of \(R(T_n)^{\rm rev}\) and the first entry of \(T_n\) are both \(1\). Consequently exactly one pair of runs merges at the boundary in (3). Using (7),
\[
|R(T_{n+1})|
=|R^2(T_n)|+|R(T_n)|-1,
\]
which is (30).

To prove (31), first use (5) and (25). For \(m\geq12\),
\[
q_m=|R^2(T_m)|=\sum R^3(T_m)
=\sum\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{m-4})+6.
\tag{32}
\]
Apply this with \(m=n+5\) and \(m=n+4\). Since
\[
T_{n+1}=R(T_n)^{\rm rev}T_n
\]
and \(T_n\neq\varnothing\),
\[
\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{n+1})
=R(T_n)^{\rm rev}\operatorname{dropLast}(T_n).
\]
Taking sums and using (5) gives
\[
\sum\operatorname{dropLast}(T_{n+1})
=
\ell_n+
\sum\operatorname{dropLast}(T_n).
\]
Together with (32), this is precisely (31).

We will also use the inequalities
\[
0\leq q_n\leq r_n\leq\ell_n.
\tag{33}
\]
They follow twice from (6). Equation (29) and \(r_n\geq0\) show that \(\ell_n\) is nondecreasing.

## 5. Exponential bounds for \(\ell_n\)

Choose \(\lambda\in(1,2)\) satisfying
\[
\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1.
\tag{34}
\]
Such a \(\lambda\) exists by the intermediate value theorem: the continuous function
\[
f(x)=x^4(x-1)^3-1
\]
has \(f(1)=-1<0\) and \(f(2)=15>0\). Neither endpoint is a root, so a root lies strictly between them.

We now construct a positive linear functional adapted to (29)–(31). For \(n\geq12\), let
\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_n={}&\ell_{n+4}+(
\lambda-1)\ell_{n+3}
+\lambda(\lambda-1)\ell_{n+2}
+\lambda^2(\lambda-1)\ell_{n+1}\\
&+\lambda^3(\lambda-1)\ell_n
+\frac{1}{\lambda-1}r_{n+4}
+\lambda^4(\lambda-1)q_{n+4}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{35}
\]
Substituting (29), (30), and (31) into \(Y_{n+1}\), collecting coefficients, and using (34), gives
\[
Y_{n+1}=\lambda Y_n-\frac1{\lambda-1}.
\tag{36}
\]
Indeed, (29) replaces \(\ell_{n+5}\) by \(\ell_{n+4}+r_{n+4}\), (30) replaces \(r_{n+5}\) by \(r_{n+4}+q_{n+4}-1\), and (31) replaces \(q_{n+5}\) by \(q_{n+4}+\ell_n\). The coefficients of all state variables then equal \(\lambda\) times their coefficients in (35); the coefficient identity for \(q_{n+4}\) is exactly (34), and the only constant term is \(-1/(\lambda-1)\).

Set
\[
c_0=\frac1{(\lambda-1)^2}.
\tag{37}
\]
This is the fixed point of the affine recurrence (36), so induction gives
\[
Y_{12+k}-c_0=\lambda^k(Y_{12}-c_0)
\qquad(k\geq0).
\tag{38}
\]

We need the coefficient on the right to be positive. First, (34) implies
\[
(\lambda-1)^2=\frac1{\lambda^4(\lambda-1)}.
\]
Since \(1<\lambda<2\), we have
\[
0<\lambda^4(\lambda-1)<16,
\]
and hence \((\lambda-1)^2>1/16\), so
\[
c_0<16.
\tag{39}
\]
All coefficients in (35) are positive, and all the state variables are nonnegative. Therefore
\[
Y_{12}\geq\ell_{16}.
\]
By (12) and monotonicity, \(\ell_{16}\geq\ell_{12}=102\), in particular \(\ell_{16}\geq17\). Thus
\[
d:=Y_{12}-c_0>0.
\tag{40}
\]

Let
\[
S=1+(
\lambda-1)+\lambda(\lambda-1)+\lambda^2(\lambda-1)
+\lambda^3(\lambda-1)+\frac1{\lambda-1}
+\lambda^4(\lambda-1).
\tag{41}
\]
All terms are positive. For every \(n\geq12\), monotonicity of \(\ell\) and (33) imply
\[
\ell_{n+4}\leq Y_n\leq S\ell_{n+4}.
\tag{42}
\]
The left inequality follows by discarding all terms of (35) except the first. For the right inequality, bound each earlier \(\ell_j\), as well as \(r_{n+4}\) and \(q_{n+4}\), by \(\ell_{n+4}\).

From (38), for \(n\geq12\),
\[
Y_n=\lambda^{n-12}d+c_0.
\tag{43}
\]
Since \(\lambda^{n-12}\geq1\),
\[
\lambda^{n-12}d
\leq Y_n
\leq \lambda^{n-12}(d+c_0).
\tag{44}
\]
Combining (42) and (44), and replacing \(m=n+4\), gives positive constants
\[
c=\frac{d}{S\lambda^{16}},
\qquad
C=\frac{d+c_0}{\lambda^{16}}
\tag{45}
\]
such that, for every \(m\geq16\),
\[
c\lambda^m\leq\ell_m\leq C\lambda^m.
\tag{46}
\]

## 6. Transfer from row lengths to row sums

Every entry in every \(T_n\) is positive. This follows from the initial rows and (3), because entries newly added by \(R\) are positive run lengths. Therefore
\[
\ell_n=|T_n|\leq\sum T_n=a_n.
\tag{47}
\]
The lower estimate in (46) consequently gives
\[
c\lambda^n\leq a_n
\qquad(n\geq16).
\tag{48}
\]

For an upper estimate, use (9) and the upper half of (46). Put
\[
C'=\frac{a_{16}}{\lambda^{16}}+ rac{C}{\lambda-1}>0.
\tag{49}
\]
This choice satisfies
\[
C+C'\leq\lambda C'.
\tag{50}
\]
Indeed,
\[
(
\lambda-1)C'
=(\lambda-1)\frac{a_{16}}{\lambda^{16}}+C\geq C.
\]
Also \(a_{16}\leq C'\lambda^{16}\). If inductively \(a_n\leq C'\lambda^n\), then by (9), (46), and (50),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+1}
&=a_n+\ell_n\\
&\leq(C'+C)\lambda^n\\
&\leq C'\lambda^{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
a_n\leq C'\lambda^n
\qquad(n\geq16).
\tag{51}
\]
Combining (48) and (51),
\[
c\lambda^n\leq a_n\leq C'\lambda^n
\qquad(n\geq16),
\tag{52}
\]
where \(c,C'>0\).

## 7. Taking \(n\)-th roots

For \(n\geq16\), all quantities in (52) are positive, so taking real \(n\)-th powers preserves the inequalities:
\[
c^{1/n}\lambda\leq a_n^{1/n}\leq (C')^{1/n}\lambda.
\tag{53}
\]
For every fixed positive real number \(u\),
\[
u^{1/n}=\exp\!\left(\frac{\log u}{n}\right)\longrightarrow1.
\tag{54}
\]
Applying (54) to \(c\) and \(C'\), both bounds in (53) tend to \(\lambda\). The squeeze theorem therefore yields
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty}a_n^{1/n}=\lambda},
\]
where \(\lambda\in(1,2)\) is a root of
\[
\lambda^4(\lambda-1)^3=1.
\]
In particular, the limit asked for in A381358 exists.
